subsubtopic: SUGGESTION PRIME MINISTER SPONSOR MEETING OF AMERICAN AND RUSSIAN LEADERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this country's two neighbours are the most powerful nations of all time, armed to the teeth with destructive potential. Canada is effectively the physical fulcrum between these two balances of terror. Both countries now have relatively new leaders, who are, hopefully, men of peace. Very recently the new Chancellor of Germany called for an immediate summit meeting. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), one of the most senior of world leaders, has remained silent on a summit meeting. Therefore, Madam Speaker, 1 move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That the Prime Minister, with the unanimous consent and urging of this Assembly, invite both President Reagan of the U.S.A. and Chairman Andropov of the U.S.S.R. for a face-to-face summit meeting on Canadian soil to strengthen nuclear detente, and initiate the process for nuclear arms stabilization and eventual reduction. I would suggest that the meeting place be Edmonton where, several years ago, Premier Kosygin held out the hand of friendship and smoked a peace pipe.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in the absence of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and in the absence of the Minister of State for Economic Development, I will direct my question to the Prime Minister.
20734

November 17, 1982
Oral Questions
On Monday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development announced a major exploration agreement with PanArctic. On that same day, the President of PanArctic said that he would have difficulty fulfilling the terms of the agreement, in part because of the decision of the National Energy Board to postpone hearings on the Arctic Pilot Project. According to PanArctic, this delay will raise costs and put the project in jeopardy, and some of PanArctic's member companies want out. In view of this situation, what steps is the Government taking to ensure that the Acrtic Pilot Project will not join that very long list of megaprojects which have been killed by the National Energy Program?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have not been made aware of the statement alluded to by the Hon. Member, but I am happy to take notice of it on behalf of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who is due in the House very shortly.
Here he is.
Oh, oh!
The instant minister.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ASSIST PROJECT
REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ASSIST PROJECT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is here now. Would the Minister comment on the actions he is prepared to take in view of the indications by the President of PanArctic that, because of the National Energy Board decision to delay hearings on the Arctic Pilot Project, PanArctic may not be able to fulfil the obligations of the exploration agreement that was announced the other day, and that unless action is taken by the Minister or by this Government, the Arctic Pilot Project will join the long list of casualties of the National Energy Program? Is the Minister free to do something else beyond babysitting the creation of his predecessor? If he is, what action will he take to ensure that some of the people who are now unemployed might be employed as a result of that project?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ASSIST PROJECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I indicated to the Press, and I am glad to have this question, that I hope the matter will be dealt with expeditiously by the National Energy Board, a body created by this House of Commons for which 1 am the minister who reports in the House. However, there are some problems for clarification by the National Energy Board before it can render a judgment.
I do hope the National Energy Board will be able to tell those participants in the Arctic gas project that they can export gas. I have discussed this problem with the National Energy Board. The Board has assured me that it has not put aside the request, but has just asked for a delay to get some more information. I hope the Board will be able to deal with
the project as soon as possible. If we can sell some Arctic natural gas to the European market and to other nations, I will be delighted.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The President of PanArctic was quoted last week in the Montreal Gazette as saying that fundamental changes to the National Energy Program are going to be required to get his company and other companies in the energy sector back to work employing Canadians. In a Canadian Press story from New York, on November 15, the Minister is quoted as saying:
The last thing we need is a period of uncertainty.
That statement is nearly right. That is the second last thing we need. The last thing we need is inertia from the Minister which will only guarantee that the tens of thousands of Canadians who could be employed in energy related projects will continue to be employed.
Is the Minister, within the context of the cabinet decision, able to exercise his responsibility as Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and do more than babysit the creation of his predecessor, and introduce some of these changes which would give some hope to those tens of thousands of Canadians who are unemployed today as a result of the National Energy Program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member likes to utter a lot of rhetoric. I have been in touch with the industry. I have been in Calgary and in New York. People understand that we have a program in place that we want to make work. I told the industry that I would offer stability and decisiveness. That is exactly what I am doing at this time. I would like to ask the Hon. Member to check with his friends in Calgary who, I am sure, will tell him that they like this approach. They know what is the name of the game. I intend to make the program work and Hon. Members can see that the 1983 predictions for the oil and gas industry are for a much better year than 1982.

subsubtopic: IMPACT ON PETROCHEMICAL PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Minister knows, I am sure, that the National Energy Program has had a disastrous effect upon the petrochemical industry and that, if it is not salvaged soon, it will collapse in a similar manner in which the oil sands and heavy oil projects collapsed. Right now something like a dozen petrochemical projects worth $3.5 billion to $4 billion are on
November 17, 1982

hold because of the heavy up front taxes caused by the National Energy Program, thus making Canadian petrochemicals non-competitive in world markets. What action is his Department taking to ensure that these projects go ahead? In other words, is he getting together with the Provinces and the industry to bring the parties together to ensure that at least some of these projects might be salvaged, in the interests of stimulating economic activity in the construction industry and thereby creating jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: IMPACT ON PETROCHEMICAL PROJECTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, many energy related projects all around the world, because of the industrial economic recession, are experiencing the same slowdown. My officials and I met with the petrochemical industry as late as yesterday afternoon to discuss their future plans. We have had a departmental task force for about the last four months, which was initiated by my predecessor, working with the industry. Needless to say, our goals are the same as the Hon. Member's, to increase jobs right across the country in the major capital projects we would all like undertaken.

Madam Speaker, the Minister and his Task Force can study this issue to death, but the fact of the matter is that it is the heavy up front taxes as a result of the National Energy Program which are making the products non-competitive in world markets. The Minister should know that and indeed does not have to study it any further.
The cancellation of the Alsands, the Cold Lake project, and other heavy oil projects, again a result of the National Energy Program, has caused the loss of tens of thousands of jobs in this country, 45,000 to 50,000 jobs in this country directly, plus the tens of thousands of indirect jobs. May I ask the Minister if he is currently undertaking any initiatives with his provincial counterparts, and with the industry, to see whether or not these projects may be advanced even on a smaller scale, given the fact that this energy source is going to be required if we are to achieve self-sufficiency? In the interests of selfsufficiency, oil security, and of creating jobs and real economic wealth, what is the Minister doing to ensure that these projects go ahead, even on a scaled down version of them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
First of all. Madam Speaker, I do not agree with the premise of the Hon. Member's question whatsoever. As a matter of fact, if the Hon. Member would take a look at our energy cost, First of all, I think right now, even our oil as feedstock is only about 80 per cent of the world price, which gives our petrochemical companies some advantage over other countries around the world. Second, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines
Oral Questions
and Resources, and I, have had several meetings with businessmen with regard to exciting energy related projects which the Hon. Member is not even aware of as yet.

Madam Speaker, the Minister is quite correct when he says the feedstock at the wellhead is certainly competitive, but it is the effect of the federal Government's tax which is causing prices to be at more than the world level, and the Minister should know that and should not try to mislead the House.
Hear, hear!

Some of these projects were onstream before the National Energy Program was thrust upon us. What action is the Minister taking specifically to see that these projects go ahead, either the projects as they were developed, or scaled down versions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the last time I looked we were not exactly responsible for initiating all these particular projects. However, as I said in my previous answer, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and I, in the last couple of weeks, have had some very fruitful discussions with consortia in the private sector with respect to some of these energy projects.

subsubtopic: TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. In his wish to use the change of leadership at the Kremlin as a means of warming up Canada's relations with the Soviet Union, and indeed I would hope reinforcing detente, is the Prime Minister reconsidering the Government's decision to fuel the nuclear arms race by testing new weapons systems and their delivery vehicle, such as the Cruise missile, or has an ironclad understanding apparently been reached with the United States that we will do such testing in return for a much larger share of U.S. defence contracts in the nuclear weapons field?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

speechtext:

I can, however, clarify this particular matter because there have been precedents in many cases during the time that I have been Prime Minister.

She appoints recipients of an honour under that Order on her own volition, without advice from the Prime Minister of Great Britain or, for that matter, the Prime Minister of Canada. November 17, 1982

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadian fishermen were encouraged this year to sell their mackerel in over-the-side sales to the Soviets through Joint Trawlers Limited of Sweden for approximately 12 cents a pound. As a result of that, Canadian buyers were unable to compete, and today long liners in Newfoundland, indeed, in all parts of Atlantic Canada, are short of bait and are forced to buy back Canadian mackerel from European suppliers.
I ask the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans how many tons of mackerel has he authorized his Department to purchase, what is the cost to Canadian fishermen, and what increased quotas did he give the Soviets, Poland or Japan, for relinquishing Canadian mackerel for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: IMPORTATION OF MACKEREL FOR USE AS BAIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is always wiser and easier to speak after the fact. Who could have predicted what happened? I am sure my hon. friend, if he knows something about fisheries, knows that no one could have predicted this situation. I have talked with the Cuban Minister of Fisheries and he told me that what happened this year with respect to the squid was something unpredictable.
What we have done is something very, very simple, and I think very wise. We have exchanged surplus offshore mackerel, which would not have been caught by Canadian fishing vessels, in order to secure bait for the fishermen of Newfoundland. I think, in view of the circumstances, the urgency of the need of the fishermen, the decision taken by my Department was the right one.

Madam Speaker, 1 have a supplementary question. I understand that the Minister did not pay for the mackerel from the Europeans. He has made available some 4,000 tons of halibut which will go to the Soviets or to Poland, and some 2,500 tons of redfish which will go to Japan in the form of quotas, in payment for these fish.

November 17, 1982
Business of the House
In light of the fact that these are high-priced species which would be worth many millions of dollars if caught by Canadians and sold to European markets, what steps is the Minister taking to assist Maritime processors who will, of course, as a consequence of this swap, lose their markets for that many tons of halibut and redfish? What steps has he taken to protect Canadian producers, following this type of deal?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think my hon. friend is distracted. What we have done is exchange allocations which were surplus in order to have bait for our fishermen. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order to bring news to the House which is very sad in nature. Today we have lost the former Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, a great family man, a great Canadian and a very good friend. He is a man who

November 17, 1982
The Late Hon. Robert Andras, P.C.
served the country well and held many portfolios in Government. Today, after a very lengthy illness, the Eton. Bob Andras passed away. I hope the House will join in sending condolences to Fran and to other members of his family.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. ROBERT ANDRAS, P.C. TRIBUTES TO FORMER MINISTER OF THE CROWN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to add my condolences to the Andras family, and to Fran in particular. I subscribe completely to what was said by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) as to the sense of duty and devotion of the former minister from that riding. As one who was in Cabinet over a period of years with Bob Andras, I want to say that he was a model of hard work and of dedication to his people. He was a man who worked very long hours, always with a sense of service, and for these reasons I am sure his memory will be treasured by all Hon. Members.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. ROBERT ANDRAS, P.C. TRIBUTES TO FORMER MINISTER OF THE CROWN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I had the privilege to know the Honourable Robert Andras as a Member of the House. I want his family to know that the Members of my Party-and many of us knew him very well- mourn his passing very deeply.
I recall him, when I was sitting in the Opposition in those days, as having been a man of great civility and kindness. He treated every person appropriately and gently. Because of a particular reponsibility that I have with respect to the Public Services of Canada, I should like to indicate that he always consulted to the fullest degree with Hon. Members of Parliament, including myself, who had an interest in Treasury Board matters and in matters affecting the Public Service. He was a model of consultation within the rules which ought to exist within the House. I share completely the words of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in extolling his virtues.
He met his end with great courage. Knowing that it was coming, he still persevered and carried on in the face of great adversity. The people of Ontario, the people of his old riding and indeed the people of Canada have lost a good servant. All members of the House of Commons indeed mourn his loss.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. ROBERT ANDRAS, P.C. TRIBUTES TO FORMER MINISTER OF THE CROWN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a Member who served in the House for many years at the same time as Mr. Andras, who worked with him and met with him frequently when he was the minister of employment and immigration, I came to realize how hard he worked and how concerned he was about the needs of the people. Among all the ministers with whom 1 have dealt, he was the most likely to listen to suggestions, criticisms and questions from Opposition Members and to give them fair consideration.
I know that Hon. Members of my Party join with me in expressing our regret on this occasion and in extending our best wishes to his family.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE LATE HON. ROBERT ANDRAS, P.C. TRIBUTES TO FORMER MINISTER OF THE CROWN
speechtext:
Certainly the Honourable Bob Andras was dear to Hon. Members on both sides of the House. As a

Of course I will transmit to his wife, Fran, the sympathies and sentiments expressed in the House.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in moving third reading of Bill C-135, an Act to amend the National Housing Act, I would like to take a few minutes just to remind Hon. Members of its purpose. The Bill will bring about certain changes in the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan which were announced by the then minister of finance in his budget address of June 29. They are as follows:
First, home owners who find, on renewing their mortgages, that their monthly payments will exceed 30 per cent of their household income will be eligible for grants amounting to as much as $3,000. Guarantees that formerly were offered to help home owners defer interest payments and reduce their monthly expenses no longer apply. Everyone who qualifies now receives the grant.
Second, home owners are entitled to the grant even if their interest is reduced at the time the mortgage is renewed, as long as their payments are still over 30 per cent. Formerly the grants were available only if interest went up. Finally, the plan is extended until the end of 1983. As the legislation now stands without amendment, the plan ended on November 12. I would like to assure Hon. Members, however, that the interest of all qualified applicants is protected. No one will be denied a grant because of the temporary lapse.
Canada Mortgage and Housing officials have continued to receive and approve applications and, as soon as Parliament provides the necessary authority, the cheques will be sent out. I would like once again to express my appreciation of the forebearance which has been shown by lending institutions in
helping borrowers during the unavoidable delays. I would also like to thank Hon. Members on both sides of the House who co-operated in advancing the Bill through its various stages as expeditiously as possible.
I am very gratified that these grants will be available throughout the coming year for those who are in serious difficulty in meeting their mortgage payments. I hope Hon. Members will bring the plan to the attention of those of their constituents who might benefit from it, and urge them to discuss their difficulties with their mortgage lenders who will explain the terms and help them prepare an application. If Hon. Members have any questions about the operation of the plan in particular cases, I know that CMHC officials, either at the national office or in the field, will be glad to help.

speakeroldname: Hon. Janies A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to assure the Minister that it is our intention to support this Bill and to support its passage through the House. Consequently, we hope that, with the co-operation of the House, and without precluding any Member from the right to participate in this debate, the Bill will receive third reading later this day.
However, having said that, I think it is incumbent upon me as spokesman for the Official Opposition to express a sense of disappointment. Here we have a new Minister who has just assumed responsibilities for housing at a time when the industry is in crisis, in fact, passing through the worst crisis since the Second World War. I do not want to go over old ground and talk about the mistakes of his predecessor. I do not want to refer to the mistakes of the June budget and the November budget, although we have to allude to them, but 1 do want to say to the Minister, knowing him as I do, that I was surprised that he did not avail himself of this opportunity to give a general policy statement on the housing situation as he sees it, and what he sees down the road in the way of solutions to the problems we are facing today. Certainly I think it is fair to say, although these matters are in the hands of the Government, that we will not have another opportunity before this year is out to discuss housing in a meaningful way, because obviously there will be no further amendments to the National Housing Act before the end of this session, or at least before the end of this calendar year.
I am disappointed because I think we had a right to expect some indication from this new Minister as to what direction he intends to take and what steps he intends to take to correct the mistakes of the past, those of his predecessor-albeit they were honest ones, but serious-and, of course, those gross mistakes of the previous two budgets. We are being denied that opportunity and, therefore, we can only try to present to the Government the concerns that we have with respect to this most important industry.
Just a few days ago, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation released the vacancy rates for rental units in this country. While we have noticed some improvement, there is nothing in those statistics to give us any reason to be
November 17, 1982

encouraged, especially when we examine the facts. We still have serious vacancy situations prevailing in some of the major metropolitan areas of the country, including this City of Ottawa. However, if you take a look at the situation, of the
61.000	units that were completed in 1981, as I understand it,
55.000	were started under the MURB Program. Now we do not have the MURB Program, we have the Canada Rental Supply Plan, to which I will refer in just a moment.
We are falling behind in terms of our requirements, and there will be another shortfall this year following the shortfall from last year, which will have a very important impact on the supply situation as well as the cost situation. I realize there are complications regarding the price of rental housing in this country which speaks to the need for some kind of federal-provincial agreement in the whole area of rent controls as they apply to the ten different provincial jurisdictions in the country. Unless we have a unified approach to rent control, I am afraid there is not very much we can do about encouraging investment in rental accommodation, the Canada Rental Supply Plan notwithstanding.
I do believe that a case could be made, and 1 make no apologies for this, for re-introducing the MURB Program as a short-term measure, a quick fix kind of response, because of its ability to generate starts in terms of rental units.
Let us take a look now at the Canada Rental Supply Plan. This plan was introduced by the Government as a means to make up for the phasing out of the MURB Program. The Government made provision for interest-free loans to finance up to 30,000 units. We already know that 53,900 units were started under the MURB Program last year. But under the Canada Rental Supply Plan, provision was made for interest-free loans for up to 30,000 units. The ceiling of $7,500, which was originally applied to the plan, has been lifted. We now know from experience to date that the average loan per rental unit now stands at about $12,000. Up to November 17-and these are the latest figures I could get-under the Canada Rental Supply Plan a total of 7,886 units had been started, are under way or have been approved, each representing an average loan of $12,000. As an interesting side note to the Canada Rental Supply Plan, when it was announced by the Minister's predecessor earlier this year, we find that in a press release dated March 23 the Minister said: "Up to one-third of the units assisted in this way would be made available to low income people under the federal rent supplement program."
That is commendable, given the cutback in the social housing commitment of the Government, but what are the actual facts, Mr. Speaker? When this Bill was going through the Standing Committee of the House, I asked, through the Minister, the Acting President of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation how many units of the 7,800 which had been committed, were under way, or applied, were designated as social units, or would fall into the category of social housing or low income housing. The response was, "Not one single
National Housing Act (No. 2)
unit" under the Canada Rental Supply Plan has been designated as social housing, notwithstanding the commitment made by the Minister in March.
I realize that what the Minister said in March in his press release announcing the Canada Rental Supply Plan and the position taken today are two different positions. What we were told in committee was this: up to a third of the units in a project could be designated as social housing units, not "will be" but "could be", which means, of course, that the Government has advocated the decision in this regard to the provincial authorities. This is something which concerns me greatly, considering what is happening to rental accommodation in this country today, in terms of the shortfall in supply, the increase in rental accommodation, and the increase in cost per unit of building the rental accommodation.
If we take a look at the experience to date, I can give as an example a project approved under the Canada Rental Supply Plan in the City of Toronto. This project contained 450 units. The average loan per unit under the Canada Rental Supply Plan was $15,000, and builders' cost per unit was $67,000. Rent per unit, for one bedroom, was $675 a month, and for two bedrooms was $750 a month. That, of course, by any yardstick, whether it is in Toronto or in the Minister's own constituency, cannot be considered low cost housing. That is expensive accommodation.
Where is the original commitment, made when the Canada Rental Supply Plan was first announced, to provide for social housing within this program to make up for the shortfall of the budget, because we know that last year provision was made for
30,000	units? In this year's budget, depending on which one we are talking about, but at least in the last budget which referred to social housing, provision was made for 25,000 units.
In my opinion, that is one of the more serious weaknesses in the program. This is an area where the Minister has a responsibility to take a look at the experience to date. As well, he has to take a look at the thrust of the program in terms of the impact it is having on starts in so far as it is supposed to replace the MURB Program. I think if the Minister takes a good hard look at that situation, he will find that the program is in fact not living up to expectations.
The experience across the country varies from place to place. Not one single unit has been approved or is under way in the Province of Newfoundland. In the Province of Nova Scotia there are 182 units; New Brunswick, 27 units; Prince Edward Island, no units; Quebec, 1364 units, and Ontario, 3800 units. It is interesting to note the discrepancy between Ontario and Quebec, areas which have the same kind of demographics in terms of metropolitan areas. In Manitoba there are 404 units; Saskatchewan, 352 units; Alberta, no units. I suppose that speaks to a program in place by the Alberta Government and also reflects the vacancy rate, which is interesting in terms of the economic situation in the country. In British Columbia ther are 1740 units. What these figures prove to me is something which we were told by the HUDAC people from the Atlantic Provinces, that this program would not be effective in the Atlantic Provinces because of the up front financing

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
requirement, and they would not be able to take full advantage of it.
For these and other reasons, Mr. Speaker, I believe very strongly that the Minister would be well advised to take a look at the Canada Rental Supply Plan to see what it is doing. If it is in fact another MURB program, let us recognize it as such. At the same time, let us also recognize the responsibility which the Government has with regard to social housing, low cost housing. It is my view, shared by my colleagues and many others in this House, that the Government is not fulfilling its obligations with regard to co-op housing, because that is an area where the Government could have an immediate impact on housing starts and would be seriously addressing the problem of low cost housing.
The Minister knows full well, as do his officials in CMHC, that demand is there all across the country for co-op housing. Philosophically, the Minister is sympathetic. Co-op housing is an excellent way of beating the inflationary cycle, which has plagued the industry in the past few years, and of reducing, if not eliminating, the uncertainty in terms of rental accommodation. The experience across the country has shown that co-op housing has been more than a hedge against inflation because not only have these units been profitable in terms of meeting their commitments, their mortgages, and so on, but they have been able at the same time to keep rates well below the prevailing market. It is understandable, then, why there would be such a demand for co-op housing.
I hope that the Minister will not let too much time pass before he takes a long hard look at these proposals, and the obligation and commitment which the Government has with respect to social housing, low cost housing. This commitment is not being discharged by any of the programs which we have in place under the new policies announced in the last two budgets. The Government, indeed, has that responsibility.
Another aspect of the Government's housing policy which we would have liked to have seen addressed by the Minister today in the course of debate on third reading of these particular amendments to the National Housing Act, is the Canada Homeownership Stimulation Plan. We know that this plan was hastily put in place, indeed, without proper guidelines. It created all kinds of administrative problems all across the country. There were no standard criteria, at least none that I could determine, during the early stages of the program. I do not fault anyone for that, because of the lack of guidelines and the haste in which it was put in place, but the fact of the matter is that in many instances the $3,000 grant was a landfall to many people. I think that if the records were examined carefully instances would be found of people who received a $3,000 grant who should not have qualified. All kinds of situations occurred. Single people applied for the grant, then got married and had the advantage of receiving two grants. Houses which were well under way were able to qualify within the terms of the starting date.
However, I do not want to be unduly critical about the program because in terms of the need to provide an immediate
stimulus and a quick reaction to a situation which was growing increasingly critical as a result of low housing starts, the Government had an obligation to do something, and at least it did this. However, the fact is that now the program is to be changed quite drastically because we now know, as a result of the most recent budget brought in by the most recent Minister of Finance, that grants available under the Canada Homeownership Stimulation Plan will apply to new housing only as of January. That is rather interesting because I find that to be inconsistent with the rationale given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in not proceeding with the mortgage reduction program, which was the subject of a study by the Lortie Commission. Lortie recommended, and the Government accepted, that it not proceed with this because it would have a distorting effect on the marketplace in that it only applied to new houses. Now we find the same situation applying to the Canada Homeownership stimulation Plan. As of January, it will only apply to new houses. I can understand the reasoning behind that, the need to try to do something about the disastrous shortfall in housing starts.
What are the facts? We know from the records that up to November 12, 1982, under the Canada Homeownership Stimulation Plan, 83,761 Canadians received grants or were eligible for them. The breakdown of that 83,761 is as follows: 28,835 were for new housing, while 54,900 were for existing housing. In other words, the bulk of the applications which were funded went to existing houses. Now that is to be changed and is to be applied only to new houses as of January.
I would like to hear the Minister, his Parliamentary Secretary or someone speaking on behalf of the Government telling us how this can be reconciled, the distorting effect of this action on the marketplace and the impact it will have on real estate sales with the Government's rationale in not proceeding with the mortgage reduction program, which was promised under the budget. I will have more to say about that in a few moments. However, let us take a look at housing starts, because that is what the Canada home stimulation program is all about. When we take a look at housing starts, we realize the magnitude of the problem. Let us take a look at what would be considered a peak period for housing starts, say, in the year 1981.
In June, 1981, there were 213,800 starts, seasonally adjusted. If we take a look at what happened in June, 1982, we found they were down to 125,000, seasonally adjusted. If we take a look at July, 1981, we see a decline from June. In July, 1981, housing starts were 180,800, and in July, 1982, there was a further decline from the previous months of that year, down to 113,000. In August of 1981 housing starts amounted to
177,000	and, of course, we know that in August, 1982, there was a disastrous drop to 89,000. Continuing on to September, 1981, housing starts took a slight increase, up to 185,000. In September, 1982, housing starts were down again from the previous month, to 86,000. These are annual seasonally adjusted starts. Just a few days ago, when the Bill was before a
November 17, 1982

committee of the House, we were told that housing starts for the year are now targeted at 130,000, which, of course, would mean a very serious situation because CMHC, by its own demographic projections, estimates that we would need
220,000	housing starts for the year. So, what are we looking at? We are looking at a shortfall of 90,000 housing starts. That will drive up, and is in fact having the effect of driving up, the cost of housing in this country. It is having a serious impact on the cost of housing in the country.
Let us consider what is happening to housing costs. The national average price for a three-bedroom bungalow has risen from $37,400 in 1974 to $76,000 in 1981. Whilst there has been a slight decline in housing prices in most of the major markets in the country, we know that as a result of the shortfall, and with economic recovery and increased demand, housing prices will rise once again. If there were ever an argument that I would use to impress upon the Government the absolute necessity of providing additional funding in the area of co-op housing, it would be based on these statistics. We have a shortfall situation which will reduce supply. That will have an impact on housing costs which we will see continuing to escalate in the country, interest rates notwithstanding. That means, of course, that there are people in this country who will not be able to find affordable accommodation. I am not referring to the public housing situation. 1 am referring to coop housing, where people can get together in a co-operative way and build and manage affordable accommodation.
I know that that is a proposition or philosophy which appeals to the Minister, who is a product, of course, of the Coady Institute and of St. Francis Xavier University. I would be the most surprised person in the world if he, as one of his first initiatives, did not make a very quick move in that direction.
I would like to move on to what I consider to be the Government's obligations with regard to the now defunct mortgage reduction program, if that is the proper nomenclature. It has had several different names during the brief course of its existence. There is no question but that the Government has an obligation, if not a legal obligation, a moral one. I will not repeat the statements made by his predecessor because they have already been placed on the record. I will not repeat what was said by the former minister of finance when he introduced this provision in his budget, because that, too, is already a matter of record. 1 will simply paraphrase all the quotes by saying that the Government made it very clear that this was a commitment of the Government of Canada and, indeed, it formed a part of the Government's advertising program. It encouraged people to go out and purchase new housing with the expectation that this program would be in place and they would be able to enjoy the advantages of a reduced mortgage. We know that under that plan, mortgage interest rates would have been reduced anywhere from 4 per cent to 6 per cent. We do not know how many people were sucked in by that as we have no figures, but we do know that there were many thousands of Canadians who took the Government at its word and either purchased homes with the expectation that they would
National Housing Act (No. 2)
be able to take advantage of this program, which they had every reason to expect would be coming down very shortly or, at least, they put off the decision to purchase with the understanding that that program would be in place. I know what the quick and immediate response of the Minister would be. He would say, "Well, interest rate situations have changed. Interest rates have come down substantially". That is true, but what assurance do we have that they will stay down? That is the problem. We have no assurance at all. This may be just an aberration, just another cyclical situation. Certainly if one is facing the prospect of making the most important financial transaction of one's life, and that is what the purchase of a house represents to the average Canadian, one will not be reassured by the experience of the past two years. You are not going to make any long-term commitments. That is what the Minister's predecessor had in mind when he went on national television and talked about insuring your long-term security, that the Government was going to proceed with that program, was committed to that program. It is only a short time ago that the Government withdrew the television advertising that included that particular program as part of the over-all Government package of encouraging people to move in and buy houses now.
Now we have a new scheme, and I am surprised the Minister could not take advantage of this debate to enlarge upon the remarks he made in the House a few days ago when he was replying to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). This is the provision whereby you can use a part of your mortgage payments to buy insurance against fluctuations in mortgage interest rates. It is a good program. It is a program that does not require any blue chip committee. It does not require any great deal of deliberation. Indeed, the Minister himself, when he responded to my colleague in the House, said this: "I want to make it clear that if the proposal is found to be desirable and supportable it is not at all my intention to involve it in a future budget but rather to try to bring it forward as quickly as possible".
I want to say to the Minister right here and now that not only does he have a responsibility to discharge the moral obligation of this Government, as epitomized by statements made by his predecessor and the previous Minister of Finance, but he also has that responsibility in terms of providing something to put in its place, because many people were expecting, and were indeed told, that they had every right to expect that the Government would put such a program in place. It is a good idea. It is an excellent idea. I hope he does not fall into the trap, the luxury of thinking that, because interest rates are now down, we have nothing to worry about.
The fact of the matter is that until the economic situation levels out in terms of the long-term, it is going to have a serious impact upon housing starts in the country and upon people making a decision to enter into any long-term or medium-term contracts with respect to mortgages.

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
I see no reason why the Minister should hesitate or why the Minister did not take advantage of this opportunity, to reopen the Act to proceed with this, or at least to lay on the Table his views on it. 1 am sure that there are studies now well under way within Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, otherwise this would not have been leaked in the first place. Otherwise the Minister would not have confirmed in his place in the House that these studies were under way, that in fact they were thinking about them. I am sure they have advanced to the point where the Minister could tell the House that the Government is not only committed to it but is in fact prepared to move without any undue haste.
The Government has a serious obligation to get on with discharging the solemn commitment it made to thousands of Canadians, who were taken in by these commitments and who either purchased a home with all of the uncertainty of the marketplace in terms of mortgage interest rates, or who in fact put off making that very important decision.
Finally, I would like to suggest to the Government that their mortgage interest rates insurance program, or whatever they call it, is the least they can do to provide some assurance in terms of security in a very uncertain marketplace, in a very uncertain world.
Let us take a look at our proposals, the proposals contained in the budget of the Clark administration three years ago. We put in place a program whereby mortgage interest rates and property taxes were deductible in the form of a tax credit. We were going to phase that program in over a period of four years, which means of course that the program would be fully operational this year.
Let us take a look at the impact that would have. If you take a situation of a $50,000 mortgage, which is about average if you are talking about $70,000 as the average price for a three bedroom bungalow, if that program were in place today and you had an 18 per cent mortgage rate, the person with a $50,000 mortgage would be eligible for monthly benefits in terms of a tax credit of $125, or $1,500 a year, or a reduction of that 18 per cent mortgage to 14.5 per cent. That is the 18 per cent situation.
Let us take a look at the impact it would have on a 14 per cent mortgage, which is about the situation we are in right now. Again, if you are talking in terms of a $50,000 home, the monthly benefit in terms of a tax credit, if you take out a 14 per cent mortgage under the program which we put in place in our budget, would again provide $125 a month, but it would mean that that 14 per cent mortgage would be reduced to a 10.25 per cent mortgage; but that program would be permanently in place and it would ensure that there would be a buffer against fluctuations in the marketplace.
That to me is the most desirable program. It is one that the Government could proceed with. It could implement it in instalments or phase it in, as we were going to do. But I have no illusions in that score. I have no doubt that the Government would not proceed in that direction because it will be seen to be implementing a program that it in fact voted against when it voted against that budget of the Clark Government in 1979.
Certainly I would hope that the Minister-and I know he is serious about this because his reputation is on the line-will give very earnest consideration to providing the House at the earliest opportunity with some indication of the direction in which he intends to take us in terms of housing policy. I would hope that he would give us some concrete indication of just exactly what he proposes to do with respect to providing some kind of insurance program to protect Canadians against fluctuations in mortgage rates, which of course would have and could have and are having disastrous consequences on the lives of many Canadians. I am not talking about foreclosures and all that that entails in terms of human tragedy. We are talking in terms of affordability, in terms of the total concept of what it costs to provide a shelter in this country today. When we take a look at continuing increases in fuel costs, in hydro costs, all of the costs identified with providing a home, we see the importance of any program that would stabilize mortgage interest rates in this country and provide some medium-term security for those who already own homes and are faced with mortgage renewals. We have about 700,000 mortgage renewals coming up annually. Those Canadians are still hoping that the Government will make it possible for them to be able to find first, affordable rental accommodation and, eventually, as was the custom in this country until the time that this Government brought in programs that changed all that, be able to look forward to the day when they can afford to buy their own homes, and buy them with the knowledge that they are protected by some program which would provide not for their long-term security but at least their medium security, say over a period of five years.
That is a commendable program. It is better than nothing. Ultimately I would prefer to see the mortgage interest deductibility plan we had, but in the face of the Government's determination not to proceed with that, I hope the Government will proceed with this program.
Finally, I say to the Government how important this particular industry is in terms of its impact on the economy. When you talk about housing, you talk about a labour-intensive industry. This industry is capable of creating jobs directly and through the spin-off.
The data indicates that for every housing unit built in this country, 2.5 jobs are generated. When you consider that 1.5 million Canadians are officially unemployed and the fact that we have a 90,000 unit shortfall in housing starts in this country, it would seem to be in the interest of the Government, and certainly in the interest of Canadians, for it to make a real effort to stimulate housing starts because of the impact it would have not only on providing affordable housing to Canadians, but in creating jobs in the process.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some ambivalence about the legislation before us. It is not that it is not supportable. The legislation in itself provides some measure of relief or assistance for certain people who are currently facing and who will undoubtedly face problems in
November 17, 1982

the future. I want to speak about the difficulties that we have seen arise over the course of the last two or three years and why this kind of legislation is really quite inappropriate.
The difficulty in this country has been that the Government has failed to come forward with a comprehensive housing policy. The Government has relegated housing to the level of luxury rather than elevating it to the level of necessity. The Government has not recognized that as one of the basics of life the providing of accommodation at a price that people can afford is a legitimate Government function.
The Government must not be a passive player but an active player in ensuring that all who live in this country are able to find accommodation within their ability to pay. No one should be required to lay out the kind of exorbitant sums that people are currently being asked to lay out, either in terms of rent or in terms of repaying their mortgage as a result of recent interest rate fluctuations.
I cannot help thinking back to when it all started in the late sixties. Those of us who were interested in housing at that time recognized that the move the Government made to phase itself out of regulating interest rates in mortgages was an inappropriate move, one which would work tremendous hardship over a long period of time.
I recall making that statement in 1968, standing in the Ontario Legislature and explaining the problems we were going to have in this country as a result of the removal of interest rate ceilings and the opting out by the Government of the role that had been previously played on holding the line on mortgage interest rates. I well recall the discussion I had as we looked at the potential dangers that would automatically come to many families who were not going to be able to keep pace with the rising interest rates. I must confess that at that point I did not foresee the 20 and 21 per cent interest rates that we achieved. When 1 use the word "achieved" I do not mean it in the sense of pride, but what was hoisted upon us by the banks and other financial institutions of this country over the course of the last 16 to 18 months. I do not think anyone could have foreseen that, not even this Government.
I think the major problem in housing is the lack of commitment by the Government. The Government is a peripheral player in the whole area. No longer is Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation involved in the building of homes. 1 am not talking about putting the bricks and mortar in place. I am talking about the motivating factor that gets homes built in the right areas, at a price people can afford with mortgages available under the National Housing Act, as was the way in the fifties, sixties and early seventies.
It is quite clear that the Government has, for one reason or another, opted out of the field and left it open to private initiative, the free enterprise side of the economic factor. The problem with that has been that people who build houses only for profit tend to stop building when the profit margin ceases to be at a level that they consider appropriate.
When people opt out we see happening what the Hon. Member who preceded me spoke about. He said the reason we are running 90,000 to 100,000 behind our demonstrated need
National Housing Act (No. 2)
is that in large part those homes were built by or under the auspices of one level of Government or another. The Government was very much involved in ensuring, in years gone by, that that percentage of the housing market now being denied the opportunity to have decent accommodation within their ability to pay is given that opportunity. The needs of that percentage were being met, partly if not totally, by a public body's initiative. That program is no longer there. To spend a lot of time speaking about these minor amendments of somewhat short duration is to do a disservice to the whole question of housing.
I am always interested in looking at the various and many housing programs that have gone before us. I listened as my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was speaking. He went through some of the programs that had emerged over the course of the last two and one half years, all of which were piecemeal, all of which were aimed at trying to meet a crisis situation as it arose. None of them addressed the larger, more important problem. We are now going to see yet another attempt by the Government, or those acting on behalf of the Government, to ease the burden without addressing the problem.
We had the celebrated mortgage investment program. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stood in this House and guaranteed me personally that it would be brought in this fall.
I recall that when I asked him this immediately after the June budget of the late and lamented finance minister, there was no question but that the proposal for secure mortgages would come forward. It was just a matter of the committee looking at the way in which it would be brought in. We would then have it, and people would once again be able to get mortgages for accommodation at lower interest rates within their means. That went by the board. Obviously the Prime Minister did not know what he was talking about. That is not unusual.
We now have another program being suggested. Now we are going to get mortgage interest insurance. Now, presumably, you will be able to buy insurance against increases in your mortgage interest rates. Let us examine that for a moment. What will that do? Will that encourage financial institutions to hold mortgage interest rates down to a reasonable level? Of course not. All that will do is to encourage those who are in high finance to push mortgage interest rates up again, because they will be able to claim that those people who owe them money can take out insurance against any increase in excess of what they consider reasonable, therefore, there will be no hardship. Well, that kind of program serves no useful purpose and is unacceptable. It does not begin to speak to the problems faced by a young family, single parent or retired person trying to find affordable accommodation. It does not do anything to ensure that there will in fact be accommodation built for those people. It does not guarantee in any way that those on pensions, fixed incomes, those whose incomes have been indexed by the Government at 6 per cent and 5 per cent increases over the course of the next two years, will be protected against exorbitant increases in their rents or mortgage interest rates. I

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
cannot help but feel that the approach this Government is taking, once again, is attractive for a few people and therefore we will pass it, but overall it serves no particularly useful social purpose. Therefore, I want to address my comments to what should be done.
If ever there was a time for the Government to decide to build houses, this must be surely be the time. The need is obvious. By every single commentator's analysis there is a requirement to build about 100,000 more units than we are currently building. Those units will have to be of a wide variety of type and size in order to guarantee that they will meet the needs of society. The only way that can be done is if the Government of Canada recognizes that it has an obligation to make sure that those needed housing units are in fact built. The Government may say to me: we can't afford it, Ian. There is no way we can undertake that kind of expenditure at this time. But, Mr. Speaker, that is just not true.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that a year ago this month-I think you were in the chair on the day I raised it- we were speaking about the need to build houses, at that point it was 100,000 units, and we pointed out that if we were to start the process now we would create something in the order of 250,000 jobs. If the Government did not feel the urge to build the houses for the sake of the people who needed them, it surely must have recognized that, as an economic initiative, it might not be a bad idea to create 250,000 jobs, jobs of all types, not only building the homes themselves, laying the bricks and mortar in place or digging out the foundations, all the on-site work which takes place, but also making the bathtubs and the copper piping and shingles, flooring, all the things that are done in small factories all across the country, which would have helped to develop a new initiative in the economy. When we suggested that, the then Minister responsible for housing-since removed, thank God-was amused by it, to say the least. He was puzzled, I think in some ways, and obviously did not understand it. I was not surprised by that. But he rejected it because we could not afford it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what would it have cost us to build those
100.000	housing units and create 250,000 jobs? It would have cost us about $5 billion. By George, that is a lot of money, I said to myself. There is no point in pretending that it is not a sizeable sum. But what do you get for $5 billion? Well, you get
100.000	houses and 250,000 jobs. You reduce UIC payments by between one and a half to $2 billion because you put those people to work. That does not sound so bad. In fact it is beginning to sound reasonable.
What else do you do? You generate perhaps around $800 million in federal, provincial and municipal taxes. On top of that, of course, you broaden the tax base in a number of municipalities. But the really interesting fact about it is that you get all the money back, every penny of it. You put in $5 billion, you get all of those benefits, and then people pay their mortgages or rent and pay the money back to you over time. I thought, how could they possibly reject that? I looked at the advisers sitting in the corner, and I asked them how could they reject that. It seems to me to be such a sensible, intelligent and
reasonable thing to do. I mean, how could a housing minister, any housing minister worth his salt, sit there and say that they would rather have these piecemeal sort of programs-adhock-ery, as my colleague says-a sort of patchwork approach to meeting the emergency, without any overview of how to meet the real problem? I can tell, Mr. Speaker, that you, together with other Members, are just sitting on the edge of your seat, thinking: my God, if only that is brought forward we will vote for it and get on with it.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that when I made that suggestion one year ago this month unemployment was 9.3 per cent. We had about 960,000 people unemployed at that point. We had a deficit of less than $12 billion. But the Government said it could not take on that additional expenditure because of the size of the current deficit. Well, 12 months have passed and we do not have the houses, but we do have a deficit of $24 billion or $25 billion; we now have close to two million people unemployed, and we still need those housing units. There is no single thing that we could do in this country, there is no single initiative that we could undertake, not one, that would create the same kind of return as doing just that one thing would create. We could have had co-operative housing, we could have had homes for the aged, we could have had rental accommodation for senior citizens, we could have had single family dwellings in many centres right across this country, and we would have reduced the number of people on unemployment by about 250,000, I predict. We would have shown initiative and created momentum. The Canadian public would have seen the benefit, they would have felt better about the Government and its approach, and we would have derived significant additional spin-off benefits. But what happened? What happened was that we got a $3,000 grant instead. We got a $3,000 grant in its place. It did not generate houses in any significant numbers. The number of housing starts continued to decline, so it is with a sense of absolute frustration that I approach consideration of this legislation.
Is the situation beyond the understanding of the Government? Is there some mental block that keeps the Government from understanding its responsibility to the nation? Dammit, we have poured money down the drain in the last year. We had to go to the aid of Dome, to the aid of Chrysler and to the aid of Massey. We had to dig into our collective pockets week after week, and month after month, but what did we get in return? Not a single job.
What I am trying to get through to the Minister, who has just taken over responsibility for this portfolio, is that this should be the last time the Government comes forward with this kind of inadequate legislative proposal. Let us begin to deal with the problem as and where it exists. For the first time, let us begin to recognize the potential there is in meeting the obvious need. Let us begin to put in place the structure necessary to guarantee that on an ongoing basis, year by year, we will make sure, by whatever means necessary, including direct
November 17, 1982

involvement, that there is the direction, the stimulus, the money, the planning needed to ensure that we meet our responsibility of providing accommodation to the public, while, at the same time, deriving the economic spin-off benefits.

If it is the will of Parliament and the Government to hold interest rates down, it can be done.

That is where he should start.

That is the way things used to be. That is the way things were done until 1968. That is the way the country met its obligation to provide accommodation for people until the late 1960s when the Government, under pressure from the Senate Banking
National Housing Act [No. 2)
Committee, made the appropriate and necessary changes to eliminate the ceiling on mortgage interest rates.
We must go back to that stage now, while interest rates are coming down. This is the time to move in that direction. I put it to the Minister that this is where he must start.
The next thing he must do is to establish the right of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to get back into the business of building and creating accommodation for people in this country. It should be involved in ensuring that accommodation of various types, funded in a variety of ways, is available in communities all across the country, and that people can get the accommodation they can afford.
If the Government does those two things and then meets with the agencies of the Provinces and municipalities to work out some sensible bylaws to govern the building of accommodation, then we will be able to assure people that houses will be available for them. This accommodation can be of the single family type, co-operative housing, accommodation in an apartment, or whatever, but there would be a sufficient stock of housing. This would hold the price within reason.
Not so many years ago when you bought a house, although its value rarely came down, equally, it did not rise by leaps and bounds, month by month. We have reached the point where investment in housing is more lucrative in terms of the realization of immediate capital gain than is investment in almost any other thing, except last year's issue of Canada Savings Bonds.
Those are the three steps that should be taken, Mr. Speaker. The Minister should begin with the money lenders and require that they make the necessary money available so that building can begin. He should establish a Crown agency capable of contracting out to all and sundry who are competent to build, the work that has to be done to erect the 100,000 units that are needed now and whatever units are required for the future. He should sit down with the municipalities to straighten out the bylaws that in many ways infringe on the ability of people to build within the price range they can afford.
If the Government did these three things, then it would have a housing policy which would last. In that event the Government would not have to constantly run back to the House of Commons asking for adjustments, amendments, minor changes, tinkering, playing around, handing out grants, taking grants away, reducing interest rates by little bits and raising them later. It would not have to go through all this because there would be a stable housing policy that builders and lenders would understand, that municipalities would be able to use and plan by, that would put people to work, that would create places for people to stay, and best of all would be within the ability of Canadians to pay. This is ultimately where the bottom line has to be drawn. People in Canada, families or singles, must be able to find accommodations within their income capabilities.
If the Minister really wants to leave his mark in his present portfolio, he should never again come forward with such legislation. It is almost offensive, considering the magnitude of
