Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to spend much time on the consideration of Bill C-135. First I should like to congratulate the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) on his appointment to a new portfolio. I should like to draw his attention to a problem which is experienced particularly in high growth areas in northeastern Alberta, such as my home riding.
There are a large number of young families who purchase mobile homes which are located in mobile home parks. Indeed, in Fort McMurray I estimate that at least 20 per cent of the population is housed in these homes, but the nature of the homes has resulted in CMHC, through regulation, denying such home owners the programs which the Minister has brought forward. I am referring to mortgage assistance programs and the $3,000 home ownership grant, for example. They are not available to these people because their homes are not pegged into the ground or they have not been erected upon solid foundations.
I should like to make the case that indeed these homes are permanent. In my experience with the largest mobile home park in Fort McMurray, some of the homes have been there ten years and will never be moved. These are homes just as one may have a house built on a lot. They move their homes on to fully-serviced lots. The roadways are paved, the curbs and gutters have been installed. By their nature these homes must be kept off the ground in order to protect the services; there must be crawl spaces. Thus it is very difficult to erect foundations on which to set these homes.
Another point I should like to make is that a number of young families, again in high growth areas, are moving onto farms or acreages. Again for ease of construction and indeed for reasons of cost, they opt for mobile homes. It could be a double-width or a single-width model. These people are denied any assistance through these programs.
It is unfortunate that we were not able to propose an amendment to the Bill, but being a money bill, I am sure the Minister is aware that we cannot do so. I would suggest that by definition or by regulation through CMFIC this injustice to many mobile home owners across the country could be rectified. I plead with the Minister to have his officials look into the matter because I think it is an injustice.
Those are the remarks which I wanted to direct to the Minister. I hope to hear from him soon on a positive note. I thank him for giving me his attention.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate today. At the outset I want to take the opportunity to extend my best wishes to the Minister in his
new job, and not in any way to chide the Minister by saying that I hope his introduction of Bill C-135 today, as a fisherman, is the low water mark in his housing ministry.
I hope we come to understand housing with a much different importance and perspective than Parliament has traditionally looked at the entire question. I want to reflect upon two aspects. One is the enormous potential for job creation within the housing industry. I believe this is something which is readily recognized and acknowledged throughout the country. The other aspect for which I believe there is not nearly enough recognition is what is, by scientific study, the correlation between adequate housing and the negative social factors in place in society today. I will dwell on that point at greater length in a few moments.
I am disappointed to know that with the enormous importance we must assign to housing in Canada, a country of a northern climate where housing is not an option but a requirement, the Minister took approximately two minutes to introduce the Bill. I subscribe to the opinions expressed earlier this day that the very essence of a house, its necessity and relationship to family and a home, and the requirement to meet the needs of Canadians, are such that a Minister, in establishing himself in a new portfolio, ought to have taken the time to outline for Canadians the broad perspective of a housing policy which they could view with some confidence for a long time into the future.
Essentially the Bill before us gives us a grant. On the other hand, we have a set of conditions where interest rates, though lower, are unusually high by historical standards. Also we have an unusually high unemployment situation and what has been referred to as a depressed or recessed economy. Given this set of conditions, grants are not the answer to stimulate housing. If the economy is downpressed and if there are unusually high interest rates, holding out a carrot of a $3,000 grant to persons to build $50,000 to $100,000 homes will help people who already have available capital with which to build homes. It will not help those people who are marginally able to exist in society. They will not find a $3,000 grant to be the difference between being able to own a home or not. It is not only the cost of homes but the cost of servicing the money which stops people from building houses today. I submit to the Minister that in large measure while there is some good in this legislation, it is unfortunately biased toward helping those who need help the least.
If we look at what we are facing with regard to our housing situation in Canada today, we note that the shortfall in housing is extreme and excessive. In each year over the past four years we have had a shortfall in housing. In 1979 there was a shortfall of 25,000 houses, according to the projected needs. In 1980 there was a shortfall of 63,000 houses, and in 1981 there was a shortfall of 44,000 houses. This year there will be another shortfall of 87,000, for a total shortfall in the four-
November 17, 1982

year period of 219,000 houses. We have had a shortfall of approximately one-quarter of a million individual houses in a four-year period.
During 1979 to 1982, though not as severe, a similar trend of numbers appears for apartment units. In 1979 we had a shortfall of 19,000 apartment units. In 1980 there was an additional shortfall of another 30,000 units, followed in 1981 by an additional shortfall of 16,000 units. This year there is a projected shortfall of 37,000 apartment units. This makes a shortfall total for that four-year period of 102,000 apartment units in Canada. It is fair to add the house and apartment shortfall together and see that over the last four years we had a shortfall total of 321,000 housing or apartment units.
That background, I believe, outlines what is a very, very serious social concern that we Parliamentarians must address. There is researched evidence to establish a correlation between adequate housing and social problems, and not just between housing and jobs. The problem trickles down to such industries as the caterpillar tractor that comes to dig the basement, the construction people who mix the cement and haul it so the basement can be constructed, all the way through to the people who do the final drapery and carpeting of the home.
The very existence of the independent detached house is a very different social environment in which to raise a family than that where a husband, a wife, two children, a parakeet and a poodle reside on the twenty-second floor of a highrise apartment. The data obtained in much of the social research done today establish that there is strong, significant correlation between the negative social behaviour that is running rampant in our society today and inadequate housing. All we have to do is take a look at the number of suicides, the number of broken homes, the health problems and the learning problems of children. Recent studies were done in Chicago and New York. A correlation was established between those people who lived in communities with higher noise levels, measured in decibels, those who live in the quieter suburban regions, and learning ability. There is also evidence that shows that causes of marriage breakdown, divorce rates, suicide and all of the rest are related to whether or not one has adequate housing.
I suggest to the Minister that he take a look at the culture of North America, the nature of detached housing, the kind of John Wayne syndrome in which we live, to see that the value of a house is simply more than just dollars and cents. It is not just the cost of the house; there is a much larger cost to society when that society is inadequately housed. While I submit that it is far more difficult to put an actual dollars and cents value on research in psychology and sociology, it is extensive enough that it requires an approach by Government to ensure adequate housing and that we should be able to guarantee to Canadians of varying income levels at least adequate housing so the family tradition can continue. As a result there will be much less demand on Government for social services.
My own Province, the Province of Alberta, has had a migration rate from the rest of Canada of more than 2,500 people per day for a period of at least four of the last five to six years. This was a tremendous boom for the Province, but the Province of Alberta today is suffering the worst of all the
National Housing Act (No. 2)
social problems with respect to rates of divorce and suicide, and much of this relates back to the fact that Alberta is also the area where one finds the tightest of housing markets in Canada today.
I would like to refer to another approach that I believe the Government might have been able to take that would have been more equitable and I think there is a significant public demand for the Government to undertake it. In Canada today we still have an 11 per cent building materials tax at a time when we have a 321,000 shortfall in housing and apartment units. That a Government can still afford to tax building materials at 11 per cent while at the same time claim that it is trying to stimulate housing is simply nonsense. This would not befuddle any grade three student, who would know that it is absolutely essential to do the opposite. Moreover, the fact should be underlined that the Government is collecting a building materials tax of 11 per cent; that works out to just short of $3,000 on the average Canadian home. In other words, $2,800 or $2,900 could be saved by the average home owner.
This Government is saying that it will give a grant of $3,000 to certain people while leaving in place the building materials tax for everyone else. In short, the Government has put in place an expensive additional tax, which means that when a person goes to his local hardware store to buy things needed to build a dog house or to fix up a fence, he is paying an 11 per cent tax. That tax should be removed. It would be a much more fair and equitable stimulus for the industry. It would also give a stimulus to the broadest sector of Canadian society and would not be limited to those people who spend only 30 per cent of their incomes on housing.
With that in mind, I suggest to the Government that is one of the approaches it ought to take, because it would have a broader perspective of fairness and would probably do more to stimulate housing than the present policy does.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to note that one of the policies brought in under the Clark Government in 1979, in the budget of the Finance Minister at that time which was defeated by the Liberals and the NDP, was to allow Canadians to write off their mortgage cost for income tax purposes. To illustrate what that formula would have meant today in terms of housing, Canadians would have been much better off as far as housing affordability is concerned than they are today under the present grant of $3,000 from the Liberal Government. What it would have meant is that for the person today who buys a $50,000 house or remortgages at approximately 14 per cent at today's rate, there would have been a rebate equivalent to $125 per month, meaning that the real interest rate on the mortgage would have been in fact reduced to ten and one-quarter per cent. If a person bought a house worth $70,000 and applied their maximum rebate, again it would be $125 a month, which would have meant an 11.5 per cent interest rate for their mortgage under that Conservative formula.

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
That kind of policy was one that the Liberals and the NDP decided to defeat. The fact of the matter is that Canadians would have been better off, housing would have been more affordable and, therefore, more houses would have been constructed.
I would like to expand on that last statement with respect to employment, unemployment and the housing industry. The housing industry is the proper place for the Government to give encouragement because it has a filtering down effect that touches the largest portion of our society. When you build a house, trees start coming down, sawmills start working, cement plants start grinding, trucks start moving, caterpillar tractors start digging, copper mines start to provide wiring, carpet manufacturers begin to sell curtains and rugs, and appliance people go into operation-the whole scenario, right through to paints and chemicals. Not only is it a stimulus that affects such a broad sector of society, but it reaches into virtually every region of the economy. That is the proper way for Government to say it will make housing affordable, by making sure the people of Canada are not hit by interest payments at the high rate at which they are now, which affects everyone's quality of living. Stimulus to housing has an enormous effect on the economy of the country.
In 1982 700,000 Canadian families had to renew their mortgages. With more and more Canadians out of work, the need for assistance from the Government of Canada becomes even greater. In October of 1982 there were 1,450,000 Canadians unemployed. I need not tell a wise person such as yourself, Mr. Speaker, that this figure does not reflect all the unemployed people. That figure is the "official" unemployed. The statistical data do not include the over 80 per cent of our native people who are unemployed, or the people who have quit looking to Canada Manpower after six or eight months of finding no work. It would not surprise me or, I am sure, most Members of Parliament, that the real figure of unemployed in Canada, with a population of some 24 million, is more probably in the neighbourhood of two million.
By way of conclusion, may I say that housing is the largest single component in our consumer price index. Any stimulus such as inflation which causes housing costs to increase has the biggest effect on our consumer price index. In the face of that important fact, this Government tells us repeatedly that their principal concern is the reduction of inflation in Canada, a goal for which I applaud them; but it makes absolutely zero sense that it would continue with the 11 per cent building tax which affects everyone, not just some groups of Canadians who find themselves in a situation where more than 30 per cent of their income goes for housing. In effect, all Canadians must pay tax on every piece of building material they purchase. Remove the tax and the economy will receive more stimulus than any grants given out to limited numbers of Canadians.
As an economic sector, residential construction is a major industry and accounts for 6 per cent of our gross national product. That, again, should signal to us the importance of stimulating the housing industry. Six per cent is no small
portion of the large volume of money which in fact would equal the gross national product. There should be an appropriate stimulus in that area. We must realize that if, as has been recognized by economists, we are in a very serious economic downturn and our gross national product is not being stimulated adequately, surely housing is one of the stimulative areas which is most important.
Finally, I would like to deal with one further fact, which is the migration patterns of Canadians today from rural to urban centres. More and more Canadians are gravitating to urban centres, to the point where the ratio is virtually reversed from the early days of our country. At that time approximately 87 per cent of the people lived in rural areas. Today it is almost that identical amount of people who live in urban centres. Most of the rural Canadians are really rural, non-farm, because actually only 5 per cent of Canadians live on farms today.
What I would like to stress, Mr. Speaker, is that there needs to be a new approach to the question of housing. There should be an approach with respect to urban centres which gets away from more and more apartments to houses which are affordable. 1 am not suggesting for a moment that the Government stop any of its activities in terms of encouraging the building of more affordable apartments, but rather that that is not in itself the answer. As long as the house is the largest single expenditure that the average Canadian family will ever incur, that house, in a North American clime, must be made affordable and accessible.
What we are looking at is a two-pronged concern. The desire of Canadians in general to own their own homes, at least some day, versus an economic set of conditions, an employment set of conditions and an interest rate set of conditions, is making it such that there must be some stimulus in our system.
The actions of the Government today amount to this. The Minister in charge of housing introduces a housing Bill, speaks for approximately two minutes, outlines no broad strategy for housing, addresses no broad concerns of housing, but simply makes some amendment with respect to a previous inequity. He leaves the Bill before us without addressing the long-term concern of housing itself.
A fundamental and root evaluation needs to take place, not just of houses, costs and dollars, but of the concept of families, the concept of family in play, the concept of family and association, the concept of the home as it relates to the structure of our society, and of all the extraneous costs attached thereto. The fact is that we live in a country which, by the standards of virtually every Canadian, provides inadequate housing at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say how pleased I am to see the Minister of Public Works and the Minister responsible for housing (Mr. LeBlanc) in the House today. I do not intend to occupy the time of the
November 17, 1982

House for long with respect to the matter, but I am pleased to see him here. I think it is an important part of the parliamentary process that when a Minister's Bill is being addressed by the House of Commons, the Minister responsible be here as much as possible.
I am also pleased to be able, on my first intervention in the debate, to extend my good wishes to the Minister as he undertakes the work in his portfolio. I note that he has sitting beside him the new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane), and I am sure he is instructing him in the vagaries of fish and seals and other things. However, his portfolio is a very important one with respect to housing because it is a difficult problem facing the country. 1 think in terms of public works that his portfolio is historically significant in the development of the country and that with respect to the National Capital Commission his responsibilities have a great deal to do with the prosperity and development of a capital which reflects all of Canada.
That is the spirit in which I want to address the Minister. I want to tell him, as he already knows, that it is our intention to support the Bill because it will be of some assistance, but perhaps not enough assistance in view of the size of the problem facing housing. However, it will give some assistance and it is a piece of legislation that is worthy of support and we intend to support it.
I hope it is helpful in one problem which I would like to address through Your Honour to the Minister. It relates to the really startling evidence that Ottawa and the National Capital Region in general now has the lowest vacancy rates in the country, according to statistics released by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In Ottawa-Hull, as it is described, the vacancy rate is 0.3 per cent, with Ottawa at 0.2 per cent and Hull at 0.5 per cent. I think that if one translates those figures, spreading them out into the Cities of Nepean and Gloucester, one will perhaps find that the figures are about the same.
It is the lowest vacancy rate, and what that means to the people in the area is that there is the gradual development, in the rental housing area in particular, of very little choice. I hope that the Bill will advance the cause of construction and will somehow entice people to invest in owner-occupied homes, which would relieve, to an extent, the very low vacancy rate with all of its ramifications. Then it would be a very healthy move.
I do not have to tell the Minister that tenants and renters in the area are caught in a bit of a squeeze. The Government has enacted the six and five program, limiting the wages of a large group of people who work in the Public Service in Canada. The extent of their income has been limited. The economy, as poor as it is, has limited the incomes of others not within the Public Service. So there is a squeeze here. Granted, we are more fortunate than other parts of Canada in many ways, but there is still a squeeze.
However, with respect to apartment rentals in the centre of Ottawa, the outskirts of Ottawa and in Nepean, people are living with limited choices of accommodation while the rents in the area have grown. It has been brought to my attention that
National Housing Act (No. 2)
increases of 18 per cent, 25 per cent and 45 per cent have been approved by rent review tribunals. I must tell the Minister that there is a dreadful uncertainty among people who rent, some who rent by choice and others by necessity. Their concern is whether or not they will be able to enjoy the standards of living accommodation to which they have been accustomed.
I take it that this is a very real problem, one which Members of Parliament from this area meet every day, and I want to address it in the following terms. I know that rent review and control in the sense it is practised, at least in the Province of Ontario, is not within federal jurisdiction but, rather, is within provincial jurisdiction. In one particular case the provincial Government has moved, although some say not adequately. The Government of Ontario has moved with respect to the City of Toronto, but the problem remains. It is endemic to the system and we hear about it every day.
I want to repeat a request which I made to the Minister some time ago that he look at the situation within the National Capital Region so that he may understand that the vast number of rental units are owned by landlords, benevolent or not, in an almost monopolistic set of circumstances which leaves little room for competition. Many people feel that they have been taken advantage of as a result of high interest rates and the monopolistic conditions which exist.
The Minister himself cannot lower the rent and I am not suggesting that he can do that. I am not suggesting that he can control the rents, either. However, as a federal Minister he has some responsibilities, as had his predecessor, to take some leadership in recognizing the problem. I am now asking the hon. gentleman, who is known for his leadership with respect to fish, to take leadership with respect to tenants. I would like to suggest to the hon. gentleman, for his consideration, that he, as the Minister in charge of housing policy for the whole of Canada, should recognize that that situation exists here in the National Capital Region but that it also exists in other cities. He should get together as quickly as possible with all his provincial counterparts to see whether or not some concerted action can be taken by all the Governments. The provincial Governments should be encouraged to take action with respect to the situation, which is getting worse.
I tell Your Honour that many people have come to me and said that not only are their choices limited with respect to housing but that they do not see any light at the end of the tunnel either. I mentioned this to him during the course of a speech I made a little earlier and I would like to take these few brief moments to bring it to his attention again. I believe he could be doing a great public service. With his reputation as a conciliator, which is a reputation that has been earned-there are many in this House who would disagree with that, but I would like to say that he has that reputation-he could bring whatever powers he has, whatever influence he has, to bear on the provincial Ministers of Housing to see whether or not there is some way that there can be a joint Government effort, or a conference at least, to explore the problems to see whether both levels of Government could work together in this area.

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
I want to conclude by saying this. Canadians generally are not organizers, they are not marchers, they are not demonstrators. What has happened in the rental communities in the country is that the Canadian people are organizing, they are demonstrating, they are marching. They are marching because of the limited choice of housing, the high cost of housing, and a sense of despair as to what the future is.
1 think that should be a signal, not just to provincial Governments, although certainly it should be a signal to them, but as well to the federal Government. I ask for that kind of intervention by the Minister. A federal-provincial conference with respect to the problems of rental housing would be something that would be welcome in the national capital and across the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate the Minister of Housing for being here today for this debate on his Bill, and 1 wish him well in his very important portfolio.
If 1 may, I would like in the time available to me to break down the subject by the problems as they appear to be, and then deal with some of the solutions that I believe should be considered by the new Minister.
The Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has indicated that the Party intends to vote for the Bill as it constitutes something positive in a very important area.
Let me for a moment give some indication of the housing problem as it appears across the country. I have in the Toronto Star of October 12 the heading: "Housing Collapse Feared If Help Stops". The article states:
Builders and constructions unions fear a collapse of the multi-billion-dollar housing industry this winter if Ottawa and Queen's Park don't give more help to new home buyers.
A little further down:
The industry, which has been hurting for almost two years, provides jobs directly or indirectly for one in every ten of Canada's workers, according to industry estimates.
From The Globe and Mail for October 29, 1982:
"Developers Warn Housing Industry Key To Recovery''
That is a sentiment I share profoundly. In western Canada it is the energy industry, but for the rest of the country it surely must be the housing industry. Continuing:
Governments are going to have to find ways to push mortgage interest rales down if the housing industry is to play its increasingly crucial role in pulling the country out of recession, a spokesman for a national organization . . . said yesterday.
Further down:
"Considering the state of the auto industry, housing will have to carry a lot of the burden of recovery," Mr. Galway said.
Thirdly, a quote from the Montreal Gazette of October 8, 1982 under the heading: "Housing Starts Reach 22-year Low". I quote:
The recession tightened its grip on the residential construction industry last month, as Canadian housing starts fell to their lowest level in 22 years-from a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 89,000 in August to 86,000 in September,
according to statistics compiled by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. (CMHC).
That's the lowest level of activity recorded since March, 1960, and appears to be further confirmation the current construction slump is longer and deeper than predicted by most experts.
Another quote from a newspaper under the heading: "Ottawa Urged to Develop National Policy on Housing".
One other short quote, datelined Winnipeg:
The federal Government must stabilize Canadian real estate markets by developing a national housing policy and indexing mortgage rates-
That was said by the President of the Canadian Real Estate Association.
A quote from the October 18, 1982 Globe and Mail, headed: "Housing Sector Banks on Cheaper Money", reads:
Ewen Ferguson, president of Construction Forecasts Co. of Toronto, describes people as being "gun-shy" because of high unemployment. And he argues that mortgage rates are going to have to come down more-to the 12 to 14 per cent range for about six months-before normal activity will resume.
A quote from The Financial Times of August 23, 1982 under the heading: "Home Ownership on a Downward Track":
For the first time since the 1960s, when baby boom families distorted housing patterns, home ownership rates in most parts of Canada are declining.
Another quote from the Calgary Herald of October 15, 1982. This is just one paragraph:
The interim report by the Task Force on Affordable Housing says home ownership-long a goal for most Canadians-is now beyond the reach of a growing number of Calgarians.
You may be wondering, Mr. Speaker, why I am telling you there is a problem in housing when everybody knows there is a problem in housing. The question, of course, is: What is the Government going to do about it?
I would respectfully suggest that the real problems of housing, at least at the moment, involve interest rates. It is true that mortgage rates have dropped drastically, from a high, 1 see in this chart, of about 21.5 per cent to 22 per cent in April of 198! to about 14 per cent today and, you may say, they may go down even more. They seem to be going down, and I hope they do by the end of the year.
1 would respectfully submit to the Minister that what is holding back the young couple or the middle-aged couple now is not the current level of interest rates, but the fear that if they go out now and buy a home, pay $20,000 to $25,000 as a downpayment, in one year or two years from now when their term runs out on their mortgage they will lose their downpayment because they think-and a number of people have confirmed this to me-that interest rates will be back up to 21 per cent or 22 per cent.
Has the Minister considered trying to encourage lenders to provide, if not a seven, a five-year term mortgage as their service to a desperately debilitated economy? Has the Minister considered trying to persuade the larger lenders to provide at least a five-year fixed interest rate mortgage? 1 was sorry I was not here to hear his speech. Perhaps he spoke about that, because 1 think at the moment that is the crucial problem facing the housing industry. It goes without saying that a 21 per cent or 22 per cent interest rate destroys the hope of
November 17, 1982

anybody of buying a home. The Minister may say the rates are down, but I think the point is that people have to be reasonably guaranteed that they will stay down for a three or five-year period.
I can think of all manner of people who have come to me in my riding, such as one young couple who bought a home and were paying about $600 a month principal, interest and taxes. They had to renegotiate their mortgage and it went to either $900 or $950 a month. They have a child, the wife cannot work, and they were literally in the position four or five months ago where they were asking how could they get out of their mortgage.
I am certain there are people in your riding, Mr. Speaker, and in that of the Minister who complain about this problem. They are concerned about losing their homes. If they buy a house today, will they lose it in three years when the mortgage runs out?
Another issue is the spread in what the various financial institutions pay their depositors and the rate at which they loan the money, for example, the prime rate. I recently saw an article in the Edmonton Journal published some time in October which indicated that the spread in all of the banks in 1972 was about two points. In 1982 the average spread is 4.2 per cent. The Royal Bank on October 6, 1982 had a spread of five and a quarter, the Toronto-Dominion five and a quarter, the Continental four and three quarters and the Bank of British Columbia five. It would not be unreasonable for the Government to approach these financial institutions and ask them to reduce their spread back two points in the national interest. We are all bleeding at this time. Therefore, it would not be too much to ask the banks to reduce their spread. How many couples might buy a new home at 12 per cent who would not buy a home at 14 per cent? If the banks would bring the spread down by two points as their contribution to the national crisis, it would help the housing industry across the country.
There are many other issues; I will just mention a couple. Everyone in this House knows that the capital flight last year was about $10.2 billion in direct investment and $8 billion disappeared from our national accounts. A soured investment entrepreneurial atmosphere drives up interest rates. It is a vicious circle. More money leaves Canada. Obviously some of that is mortgage money. With the exchange rate on the dollar we need more incentives to keep money in this country. A soured investment climate is our problem.
I wish to refer to a proposal made by a small builder in my riding. He has been building homes in the Edmonton area for 20 years. He points out that the unemployment rate is officially 12 per cent. In Alberta it is 8.5 per cent, which seems to surprise some people.
Let us look at housing starts. I realize I am not supposed to refer to charts. However, let us follow housing starts from 1976, when they were running at about twice what they are now, through to the present rate of about 76,000 units a year.
National Housing Act (No. 2)
In addition, let us look at the growth in unemployment from the beginning of 1981 to the present.
There is a definite causal relationship. The Minister may say the reason there are not more housing starts is unemployment. However, as my constituent points out, virtually everything in housing is labour-intensive. The copper is in the ground, the trees are in the forest. In fact, most products used to build houses come from the ground or our forests. It is simply a matter of taking them out of the ground and the forests and bringing them to the site of the new homes.
This contractor points out that more than two jobs are created with every housing start. I will not go through the details of his formula. However, he points out that if 200,000 homes more than are expected to be started this year were built, it would create 400,000 jobs. That is 400,000 men and women who are now drawing unemployment insurance or social assistance. Think of the saving to the Government if these people came off unemployment insurance or social assistance. The ballpark figure that a construction worker earns is $20,000 a year. An unemployed construction worker now receives about $800 maximum in unemployment insurance. If these 400,000 were taken off unemployment insurance, they would again have self-respect and there would be reduced social problems. In addition, they would be paying taxes and we would have the necessary homes provided.
I have an aunt who lives in a major city in this country. She is the widow of an artist. In fact, her husband painted the portrait of Sir Wilfrid Laurier which is in the lobby. She lives in very modest circumstances. However, she has had an indication that her rent will be increased 15 per cent next March. Unfortunately, because her husband was an artist, she docs not receive a pension. I am sure there are hundreds of thousands of people in similar circumstances in this country.
To get back to the proposal by this contractor, if an additional 200,000 homes were started, this would get Canadians back to work. It would get our suppliers, lumbermen, architects and engineers back to work. People who come to western Canada from other parts of the country find they are the last to be hired and the first to be laid off because of the construction collapse.
It may be said that this is all very well in theory, but can it be done in practice? I understand that in 1948 West Germany decided that the best motor for its economy was the housing industry. Ludwig Erhardt and others in West Germany decided that they must get the construction industry going. They decided that if Helmut Schmidt, for example, would donate a portion of his wages to a government-sponsored housing bank, a certain amount of that would not be taxed. It was similar to our RRSP. As a result of that proposal, all kind of money went into the pool. This money was loaned to builders at reduced interest rates. The number of homes under construction went from 200,000 a year to in excess of 400,000. I believe it stayed at that level up to the present time.
There are many men and women in this country who would like to apply their skills and trades. At the moment a great number of them cannot do that. The Government should

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
consider something imaginative, such as the West Germany plan. For that matter, what about something like our proposal to make mortgage interest and property taxes deductible? Possibly even shelters should be deductible up to a certain point. France does it. That country has a very imaginative scheme which provides subsidies to couples, depending on their income, number of children and that sort of thing.
Aside from the problems I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, the problem is volatile interest rates, interest rates which are too high, and mortgages of too short a term. 1 respectfully ask the Minister, because he is starting a new area, why will he not look at some of these imaginative programs which have worked elsewhere and consider putting them in place in Canada?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 ask which one of us in this House would deny that housing is the most readily available motor which can get our people back to work right across the country? 1 think everybody accepts the truth of that. Why, then, in a situation like this, do we have a Bill which, in my respectful submission, is a positive step, yes, but one which does not get at the basic problems?
Perhaps someone on the other side will speak to some of these matters I have raised because they are the major problems right now, and the fastest way of dealing with the problem of housing would be to deal with each of the issues I have mentioned. I hope the Government will bring forward something dealing with those matters; if it does, we can get our housing industry back to work.
When 1 was speaking about my constituent's proposal, Mr. Speaker, 1 did not mention that he maintained that by getting 200,000 homes going, the federal and provincial Governments could gain a net amount of as much as $10 billion a year. If the Minister wants to know how my constituent arrives at that, 1 would be happy to give him the figures. My constituent mentioned that more than two full-time jobs are created for every home begun because almost all the money which goes into housing, apart from land, is for labour. In short, it is the most labour-intensive industry of all. I put it to Hon. Members that the almost Siamese-twin relationship between unemployment and housing starts is striking, and housing really does appear to be the best available domestic motor to get our entire economy going again. I would urge the Government to make some significant innovations in that area as quickly as possible.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House today with a great deal of concern and without any great deal of pleasure to speak on the subject matter of this debate. I would like to reflect on the position of someone who wanted to buy a home at the time I was first married and needed a home. At that time the expectation was-it was almost a promise-that any individual who was frugal and ambitious could look forward to owning their own home in a reasonable period of time. That home would cost them roughly 20 per cent of their income. I feel that my generation and this
Government have now put the would-be home owner in a position where he has to spend not less than 30 per cent of his income, and probably 35 per cent of his income, to own a home of comparable quality to that of the home which I was virtually promised by the economy of my country when I bought it.
What pleasure then, Mr. Speaker, can I get in addressing the subject of home ownership when we as a country, and the people on your right as a Government, have allowed the value of one's earnings to deteriorate to that point?
Now, one may say that yes, you can still get by at 20 per cent or 25 per cent. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if you spend in that range as a percentage of your income, you are going far below the standards of those people who were buying their homes when I was buying mine. We have, Mr. Speaker, by our policies put home ownership virtually out of reach of even the most frugal and most ambitious of people today. When I compare that with what I inherited from my country, it is obvious that we have been very, very sloppy in our management of the economy, particularly as it relates to housing.
The Minister and I both come from communities in which, when we were young men, it was the expectation, usually realized by 90 per cent of the people, that we would be in our own homes. Certainly it approached that percentage in the smaller towns and rural areas of the country in the 1950s or 1960s. But we have denied that opportunity to Canadians, Mr. Speaker. We have changed the ball game at various levels of Government. When I purchased my home, the street on which it sits was in and paid for by the municipality or the Province. But today, Government at the municipal level has changed that to the point where you build your own streets and supply your own services, all at the highest possible cost, which in turn has inflated the cost of home ownership. Surely we have served succeeding generations very, very poorly.
I must say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this housing crisis which exists in Canada today is a black mark on the escutcheon of the Government of this country, which is approaching the criminal in its negligence, lack of leadership and forthrightness with the people of Canada as to whither are we going. It is not that long ago that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in seeking re-election, was able to say that this country is strong. Well, I want to say it must have suffered from malnutrition or something because it is very, very weak today.
There is no more stark and realistic example of that than the lack of attention to those who follow us and their right to own a home. And is it not reflected in our economy? We have a declining level of house construction in spite of all the incentives provided by the federal and provincial Governments in the form of non-taxable grants, interest-free loans or other incentives.
According to an article in The Globe and Mail, as late as October statistics indicated that we still did not have the
November 17, 1982

upsurge in house building that would make a major contribution to the improvement of the economy. No one is confident that they will be able to sell their house and get their money out of it if they are transferred. As a matter of fact, those who bought houses in the last ten years-except in Ottawa or half a dozen or so other prosperous communities-may have had to suffer a capital loss if they were transferred. In some cases this loss was absorbed by the employer. It is an economic tragedy that we find ourselves in this position, Mr. Speaker.
I do not plan to belabour the subject or to bore the Chair or other Members of the House about this. As participants in Government, while we on this side do not have any influence on policies, I feel that we will have acted as traitors to the generation to come if we compare what we inherited from the country to what we will pass on to the young people who hope to buy a home today. What a tragedy it is.
I should like to deal now with some of the difficulties that I have with the housing program. For one thing, apparently by regulation a church cannot build a home and enjoy the benefits of this program. By virtue of some regulation, this category is excluded. A couple of congregations in my constituency have approached me about this. It is rare that such a house would be vacant or for rent. I appeal to the Minister to examine the regulations to see if church congregations cannot be made eligible for the tax-free grant if they wish to build a parsonage.
1 think the regulations that apply to tenants who wish to buy the home they occupy should be amended to recognize the tenant's status, without splitting hairs. I know of a case where, by the grace of the parents, a young couple live in a home in which they have absolutely no investment. They have maintained and heated it but have not contributed to the purchase price. If they qualified for the grant they could buy the home. It was easy for me and all of my generation to do that, and I think these young people should be given some consideration so that they could buy this home. Let the churches build a home and let anyone who has no equity in a home buy it under whatever terms may apply.
It has already been stated that people living in mobile homes on rented or community lots have difficulty getting the grant. The specification that the home must sit on a basement cannot be met if one is leasing from the community or from a private entrepreneur. The regulations should take the needs of all people into consideration. 1 do not think we have any right to put constraints upon anyone occupying a mobile home. Many people have been stung in the sale of their property when they had to move from one community to another. Someone who owns a mobile home could at least take it along at little cost and not get stuck with a capital loss.
My own sons and daughters have experienced serious capital loss in purchasing homes and selling them in one community after another as their jobs necessitated. I rather admire those who are willing to start out in a mobile home and I do not think the regulations should preclude this type of shelter for those who want to buy it, regardless of location.
National Housing Act (No. 2)
I hope the Minister will address some of the inequities that result from the classifications set out in the program. I hope the regulations will be released quickly. If they do not comply with the needs of the parsonage, the mobile home and others, I hope they are not so fixed in stone that they cannot be adjusted so as to be equitable to all who want to buy a home under the program.
With that plea to the Minister I say, let us get on with this. The Bill was introduced on June 29 but the regulations are not available as yet. That is not the fault of the Minister, of course; his predecessor was extremely lax in his duty. I hope that the present Minister is more cognizant of the needs of the people than was his predecessor, who neglected these things. I suppose the secondary role that he now occupies in Cabinet shows that this was recognized by the Government.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say that I hope to finish my remarks a few minutes before six so that the legislation can be passed.
Like other Members of the House, Mr. Speaker, I support this legislation, but it is still just a band-aid solution to a very difficult problem.
Before I go further, I want to congratulate the Minister on his appointment to this portfolio. I do not envy him, as it is a very difficult portfolio. Nothing he may do will be enough for the people of Canada. In the second half of the 1970s I spent several years as a Minister of Housing in a provincial Government so I know that the problems never disappear; they are always there.
The real problem today is not one of supply of housing but of affordability. Since World War II there has been no greater success story than that of the manner in which Canadians are housed. I say that with all the honesty at my disposal. At the present time we are the best housed people in the world. Indeed, the percentage of total income that goes to housing in this country is one of the lowest in the world.
In this country we have what is perhaps the greatest ratio of single family housing to multiple housing of any country in the world. We have built tremendously expensive communities which have a very low population density and extensive facilities. At some point we are going to have to pay the price for all this, and I feel that time is close upon us. A whole new policy on housing is needed. Some of us who were provincial Ministers or federal Ministers in 1978 recognized how desperate the need was.
There are basically five areas of the total housing picture that must be addressed. The first is global capital financing. Plenty of that is available in Canada today as savings have never been higher. The money is there but the cost of that money is too high when it is required for housing.
The second matter is the delivery process. The third matter is the approval process, and the fourth is the servicing process, which involves various utilities over expansive land areas upon

November 17, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
which housing is built. The fifth matter is affordability, which is a critical matter in the area of housing.
How many people can afford housing today? 1 would ask the Minister whether this particular program of a $3,000 grant per housing unit is to help affordability, or is it an attempt to stimulate the housing industry and to create jobs? If it is both, as he gestures, that is fine; it will not do very much, anyway. What the Minister has in terms of a good program is the housing repair program.
The housing stock in the nation is such that the present occupancy rate in Canada is three persons per housing unit, and in some areas it is lower. By itself that is the lowest in the world in terms of numbers of people per housing unit, but there is some doubling up and tripling up taking place at present because of costs, particularly operating costs.
I should like to deal with the idea of a shelter allowance directly to the person, but time does not permit me to do so. I am not referring to a one-time housing grant, but to a shelter allowance directly to the person or indeed through the income tax system to provide rental rebates, as is being done in the Province of Alberta. There are many systems to assist people directly with respect to affordability of housing; many have been tried in Canada.
Again I put before the Minister the report of the provincial Housing Ministers and the then federal Minister as a result of a conference which was held between January 31 and February 1, 1978. It was literally the first sectorial conference sponsored that year and was initiated by the provincial Governments rather than the federal Government. Yesterday 1 heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) dwell on the fact that provincial Ministers never put meat on their programs when they come before the federal Government at a federal-provincial conference. There has never been more meat or thought given to the entire housing picture or the new direction of housing in Canada as it should evolve with respect to affordability, delivery, servicing and every other aspect of housing, than was put forth by the provincial Ministers unanimously in 1978. To a large degree they were approved by the then Minister, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet).
What happened? Even the projections put forth at that time are very relevant in today's picture. They knew what was happening in terms of supply and in terms of interest rates. They outlined the situation eminently well. Their first projection was that upward pressure on interest rates would develop as a result of national and international economic influences which would affect housing affordability. We knew that in 1978 without equivocation.
Also they came forth unanimously with policies on global funding and on the extension of the capital cost allowance. There were unanimous suggestions or directions with respect to funding mechanisms for federal grants to municipalities, which is an area upon which I want to touch very briefly. There was a unanimous recommendation, not for mortgage interest rate deductibility, which was a subsequent Progressive
Conservative policy, but for deductibility of property taxes from income to reduce the federal income tax and, therefore, provide some taxation breathing room to municipalities. Today the municipalities are strapped for funds and strapped in their ability to raise property taxes. They have risen by a factor of four or five over the last several years.
In regard to the entire area of infrastructure and the tremendous load of high interest rates on the capital cost of housing, I suggest that the Minister should permit the municipalities to issue tax-free bonds so that they could instal infrastructure, purchase land for social housing and become involved to a much greater degree in that area. What is wrong with municipal tax-free bonds directly associated with financing of housing and community development? I do not mean tax-free bonds for municipalities on all their other expenditures; only tax-free bonds for supplying accommodation and services to the housing they build within their respective jurisdictions.
Tax-free bonds are not a new idea. They worked in the United States remarkably well. They serve to reduce the price of housing, to provide proper utilities and proper community development. Indeed, municipalities can therefore borrow at significantly below the market level of interest rates; under today's interest rate climate, some four percentage points below the going interest rates for money.
The federal Government will have to address itself to the borrowing capabilities of Canadian municipalities in relation to having ability to provide municipal services.
I want the Bill to pass this evening, so I will not hold it up beyond six o'clock. It is an important Bill even though it is only a band-aid solution. The role of the federal Government in assisting municipalities on a selective basis across the nation will indeed have to be increased. The load on home owners because of energy price increases will have to be reduced. For example, my energy costs have risen by five times, even in Alberta, in the last four years. The cost of maintaining a home is now very high because property taxes, energy costs, utility costs and interest rates are very high. Even if interest rates come down, the cost of servicing a home, because of high energy costs, high property taxes and other ancillary cost items, will be very high. Therefore the repeated demand for housing from here on will drop significantly, and the 278,000 housing units built each year in the latter half of the 1970s will never occur again, unless our population rises explosively. This will not occur. Our population has stabilized. The average age has risen to 28 years. Indeed, the extent of immigration allowed into Canada is being curtailed.
I would have liked to speak for 30 to 40 minutes on this matter, but in the interest of passing the Bill and getting these moneys out to home owners, I will conclude my remarks at this point.
